source.title: Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules
source.authors: Jiaxiang Li; Zhi-Qi Bu; Shi-Yun Xu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure-axis and equation formatting is flattened, so several plotted values are not recoverable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures validation loss across compute and model-size sweeps, using its own training setup rather than reproducing the original scaling-law recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many dynamic-versus-static batch-size comparisons, downstream benchmark scores, and fine-tuning results. Those compare batch schedules rather than test the claim versions about scaling laws, extrapolation, or downstream predictability. Figure 5's loss-versus-compute fits and loss-versus-model-size fits are recorded below. Cited scaling-law results and the schedule values used to define the experiments are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study is about batch-size schedules, not scaling laws. Its Figure 5 still fits power laws of validation loss against compute at fixed TPP for dense Llama3 and Qwen3 MoE models trained with Muon-NSGD and WSD, with static and dynamic batch sizes. That is a new-setting result on the compute part of V1. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a convex-optimization characterization (eq. 2.5) predicts loss from learning-rate and batch-size schedules. It yields a closed-form optimal batch-size schedule that depends only on the LR schedule shape and budget, not on peak LR, model size or optimizer. This schedule consistently beats static batch size, with 6–15% compute-efficiency gains in joint scaling laws, while preserving universal (supercollapse) dynamics. The advantage vanishes under bf16 half-precision and shrinks with larger base batch size.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates learning-rate and batch-size schedules, including dynamic batch-size comparisons; it does not reproduce the original parameter/token scaling-law experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that the dynamic-batch-size advantage can vanish in half-precision training, diminishes as base batch size increases, and varies across learning-rate choices and schedules.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalized loss curves collapse across Qwen3 MoE sizes (0.4–2B) at fixed TPP=100 with scaled hyperparameters. The collapse holds for both normalized iterations and normalized tokens, under the dynamic batch-size schedule.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Universal loss-curve collapse ('supercollapse') across model sizes holds at fixed TPP under scaled hyperparameters.

fits_no_version.finding: The dynamic batch-size schedule gives a constant-factor compute-efficiency gain (1.15x Llama3, 1.06x Qwen3 MoE) without changing the loss-compute exponent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch-size schedule shifts the scaling-law prefactor but not the exponent.

record.problems: The compute fits are reported for limited model-family and TPP settings, and the paper does not establish small-run extrapolation. Figure 5's fitted equations have flattened exponent formatting in the supplied text; fit coefficients for the model-size curves are not stated. No confidence intervals or other uncertainty estimates are reported for these fits.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were omitted. Dynamic-versus-static batch-size validation and downstream benchmark comparisons elsewhere in the paper do not test the named claim versions.

untested.parts: Scaling over several orders of magnitude; separate parameter-count and token-count power laws. Compute is varied jointly with N at fixed TPP over a narrow range.
All: no fit on small runs is used to predict much larger runs.
All: only one IsoFLOP budget (1e20), and no reported optimum N or D vs compute.
All: depth and width co-vary with size, and there is no fixed-N shape comparison.
All: the VLM and math fine-tuning experiments report no scaling fits.
All: downstream scores are compared only between batch schedules at single sizes.
Not tested by design. Exponents under static vs dynamic batch size are nearly identical (0.097/0.097, 0.058/0.056), but no fitting-choice comparison is made.

missing.what: The compute range and the model sizes included in each Figure 5 power-law fit. The Qwen axis spans roughly 1e20–4e20 FLOPs; the Llama range is unclear. The text says budgets go 'up to 1e21 FLOPs'.
missing.locator: Figure 5 middle/right columns; Section 4.1; Appendix B.3

record.verdict_notes: The power-law fits are a by-product of a batch-schedule study. The fits have no irreducible-loss term and no uncertainty, and N and compute co-vary at fixed TPP. Dense and MoE exponents differ (0.097 vs 0.058), but TPP and architecture also differ, so this is not a clean V7 test. The left column of Figure 5 plots perplexity with a quadratic fit in log(model size), following Hoffmann et al. The record's tranche was changed from T2 to T3 because the study is not aimed at the scaling question.

versions.untested_parts: The compute-scaling component is tested. Token scaling is not tested. For parameter count, the paper says it fits quadratic functions of log(model size), rather than reporting a power-law fit; the results do not establish a parameter-count power law. The reported sweeps do not establish behavior over several orders of magnitude.
No experiment fits laws on small runs and evaluates predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
The study optimizes batch-size schedules, not the compute-optimal parameter-count and token-count allocation described in this version.
The study does not compare depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count to test their effect on loss.
VLM and fine-tuning experiments compare batch schedules, but do not test whether power-law forms hold in other modalities or training regimes.
The paper reports downstream benchmark outcomes but does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not compare scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations across fitting choices, parameter-count conventions, datasets, or schedules to test the stated fit-dependence claim.

rows.subject: Llama3
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss against compute FLOPs across model-scale runs.
rows.measure: Validation loss versus compute FLOPs; reported power-law fit.
rows.note: The paper says power laws are fitted between validation loss and compute FLOPs. The equation's exponent sign is unclear in the flattened figure text; the plotted loss decreases as compute increases. The fit aggregates runs at different sizes.
rows.check: The exponent is printed without its sign in the flattened text. Plugging in C=1e20 gives 244.963*1e20^-0.097 ≈ 2.81, which matches the plotted loss, so the fit is a decaying power law (C^-0.097). The compute range is not stated; the axis appears to span well under one order of magnitude near 1e20. 'Baseline' should be 'not applicable'.

rows.subject: Llama3

rows.value: A quadratic function is fitted between validation loss and log(model size); coefficients not stated.
rows.note: The text identifies the fit form but gives no coefficients or direct comparison with a power-law fit.
rows.check: This is an IsoFLOP curve at a single 1e20 budget: loss/perplexity vs model size fitted with a quadratic in log N, peak LR 0.01. At fixed compute, data becomes the bottleneck for large N, so it does not measure V1's parameter power law. With one budget it cannot give V3's optimum-vs-compute trend. No coefficients or optimum are reported.

relationships.condition: Dense Llama3 (TPP=50) and Qwen3 MoE (TPP=100), Muon-NSGD, WSD, static and dynamic batch size, compute around 1e20 FLOPs
relationships.reason: Loss vs compute fits as a decaying power law with R²≥0.998 and exponents -0.097 (Llama3) and -0.056/-0.058 (MoE), R1–R4. The narrow compute range leaves the multi-order-of-magnitude claim untested.
relationships.display_finding: Compute power-law fits achieve R²≥0.998, with exponents −0.097 for Llama3 and −0.056 or −0.058 for MoE over the narrow tested range.
